claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by maintaining a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure.
A homogeneous, single-phase microstructure prevents deleterious grain-boundary segregation.
A homogeneous, single-phase microstructure prevents deleterious intermetallic precipitation.
Sluggish diffusion during annealing delays the formation or coarsening of brittle secondary phases.
Delayed formation or coarsening of brittle secondary phases preserves toughness.
Increasing annealing temperature while holding atmosphere and duration fixed promotes greater atomic mobility.
Nanoscale grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic phases act as stress concentrators.
At lower annealing temperatures, sluggish diffusion minimizes elemental segregation and preserves a homogeneous microstructure.
Preservation of the homogeneous microstructure at lower annealing temperatures maintains high toughness.
Above a critical annealing temperature, accelerated diffusion promotes elemental segregation.
Above a critical annealing temperature, accelerated diffusion promotes nucleation of brittle intermetallics at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation and brittle intermetallics provide crack-initiation sites and reduce toughness.
Alloys annealed below the critical temperature will retain high fracture toughness and exhibit minimal microsegregation.
Alloys annealed above the critical temperature will show a significant toughness reduction together with detectable grain-boundary phase transformations or precipitate formation.
The proposed behavior applies to high-entropy alloys with comparable compositional complexity and diffusion characteristics when diffusion is the principal driver of microstructural evolution.
The proposed behavior may not apply to alloys with substantially different alloying elements or at extremely high temperatures where other mechanisms dominate.
